official_measurement_examples.name: Section 247 prerequisite
official_measurement_examples.fact: DfT guidance says a Section 247 stopping-up order enables approved development and normally requires granted planning permission or evidence the works are permitted development.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 253 sequencing
official_measurement_examples.fact: Section 253 allows the stopping-up process to start while a planning application is in progress, but DfT says the order cannot be made until planning permission has been granted.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 248 scope
official_measurement_examples.fact: DfT guidance describes Section 248 as addressing highways providing private means of access where they cross or enter the route of a proposed new or improved highway.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 249 applicant
official_measurement_examples.fact: National Transport Casework guidance says Section 249 pedestrianisation applications must be made by the local planning authority.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 251 sequencing
official_measurement_examples.fact: For land held or acquired for planning purposes, DfT says a Section 251 order cannot be made following a compulsory acquisition until the Secretary of State has been notified that acquisition occurred.

official_measurement_examples.name: Section 261 temporary use
official_measurement_examples.fact: DfT describes Section 261 orders as temporary stopping up or diversion for mineral extraction, with restoration expectations at the end of the period.

official_measurement_examples.name: All public rights of way are highways
official_measurement_examples.fact: DfT stopping-up guidance states public rights of way for vehicles, horse riders, cyclists or pedestrians are highways for this process.

official_measurement_examples.name: Application fee
official_measurement_examples.fact: DfT's current stopping-up guidance says the Department does not charge a fee for applying for and processing stopping-up orders.
